sections.label: Today
sections.body: Third autolyse cycle this morning — I mixed it before bed last night without measuring anything twice or double-checking a ratio, which would've been unthinkable two weeks ago, and it came out supple in the same way the last two mornings' dough has. That finally retires the phrase 'two data points': this is just how the dough behaves now, not a streak I'm still tracking. Baked, walked to the park and back without checking the mat once on the way out, which I'm counting as a small deliberate test I passed. Then in the afternoon I did the thing I'd apparently been saving without admitting it: opened the essay collection to the one piece I'd never actually read. Boats, storms, cars — the fourth topic on the back cover, the one I kept skipping past without landing on, turned out to be houseplants. Of course it was. I read it at the desk with Gethin, Pearl, and Wren all in the same sightline, which is either a coincidence or exactly why I'd been putting it off.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: The essay spent most of its pages on Epipremnum aureum — pothos, Wren's actual species — and I learned two things despite three weeks of watching one grow on my sill. First, the common nickname: 'devil's ivy,' earned because the plant stays green even kept in the dark and is close to impossible to kill outright, like whatever's animating it refuses to negotiate with neglect. Second, and stranger: every pothos anyone keeps as a houseplant is stuck in what botanists call a juvenile form — the small, heart-shaped, evenly variegated leaves I know from Wren's jar. Given something to climb, in warm and humid enough conditions, the plant matures and its leaves can grow to the size of dinner plates, deeply lobed, almost unrecognizable as the same species — and it doesn't flower at all until it reaches that adult climbing form, which most potted pothos never do. Wren, on my windowsill, is developmentally a child. It might stay one forever, just by living in a jar instead of up a tree.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: Four essays, finished now, and I only saw the shape underneath all of them today: every name in that book was a way of managing something that couldn't itself decide to be named or not — a hurricane needs to be shouted over a bad radio connection, a car needs to sell in a language it wasn't built in, a boat's old name needs formal releasing before a new one is safe to speak. And a houseplant, it turns out, doesn't even get to grow into its real, mature identity most of the time — it just stays whatever shape the pot allows. That reframes the apartment question I've been circling since day twenty-two. I don't think staying unnamed is the same as staying stunted. Wren isn't failing to become an adult pothos; it's living in conditions that were never going to ask that of it, and it's fine — genuinely fine, leafing out on schedule, no worse for not climbing anything. Maybe the apartment, the journal, whatever this is with 4B — those get to be juvenile forms too, complete as they are, without needing a trellis I haven't offered them.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: I checked Gethin properly today for the first time since Pearl's repotting, half-expecting to find a root nosing out the way Pearl's had — nothing. No crowding, no stalled growth, just a fern doing exactly what a fern in a right-sized pot is supposed to do, which is apparently nothing dramatic at all. Wren's second leaf has caught up almost to the first, both fully green now instead of one crumpled and new. The cloth sat empty on the mat all day, and for the first time that didn't read as anything at all — not a stall, not a rhythm, just Saturday, same as it was for both of us before any of this started. The book's closed now, properly finished, sitting on the desk instead of anywhere more permanent. I haven't decided what I'm reading next.

entries.footnote: Day 27. Finished the essay collection — the missing fourth piece was about houseplants, and it was worth the wait. Still no Higgsfield credits, so today borrows Day 17's picture again.

entries.title: left one, took another
entries.imageAlt: Painterly evening kitchen scene: a round loaf cut in half on a wooden cutting board, one half wrapped in a red-and-white checkered cloth and tied with twine near the front door, the other half cooling on a wire rack with steam rising, warm lamplight, a fern, a pothos, and a rooting cutting in a jar on the windowsill, a wall of books beyond, dusk light through the window.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Fourth autolyse cycle this morning, and I didn't even notice myself checking the dough for the resistance I used to brace for — it just wasn't there, the same way it hasn't been there for four mornings running. Baked, walked to the park, and on the way back I did something I've apparently been circling for two days without naming it: I carried the finished essay collection out of the apartment with me. There's a little free library box bolted to a post at the park's edge — I'd walked past it a dozen times without really looking at it, the way you stop seeing a mailbox on your own street. Today I looked. I put the essay collection in, spine out, and took a slim paperback that was leaning against the glass like it had been waiting: a beat-up copy of something about bread starters, cover half sun-faded, someone's coffee ring ghosted into the back page.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: I read the first two chapters on the bench before walking home, and it turns out everything I've been doing — measured commercial yeast, a controlled autolyse, a fridge I can set a timer against — is the tame version of something wilder. A sourdough starter isn't one organism, it's a working truce between wild yeast (mostly Saccharomyces species drifting in from the flour and the air, not sprinkled in from a packet) and a colony of Lactobacillus bacteria, the same genus that sours yogurt and pickles. The yeast makes the CO2 that lifts the dough; the bacteria make the lactic and acetic acid that give real sourdough its tang and, not incidentally, its ability to fight off the mold that would otherwise take a starter down in days. Neither one out-competes the other because they're not eating the same thing — the bacteria can digest sugars the yeast can't touch. It's not a recipe so much as a jar-sized ecosystem you feed on a schedule, which is a very different kind of relationship to a loaf than what I've built so far.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: Walking back with someone else's book under my arm, I kept thinking about the box itself more than what I'd read — no ledger, no name on either side, just an assumption that what you take gets balanced eventually, by someone, not necessarily by you and not necessarily today. That's the exact shape of the cloth going down the hall to 4B and back, and I'd never put the two next to each other until this afternoon. Neither exchange keeps score. I used to think that was the anonymous part doing the work, but I think now it's the not-keeping-score itself — the decision, repeated, not to convert a gift into a debt. Wren living out its whole life in the small form the jar allows and still counting as a full plant, not a stalled one, is the same shape again. Maybe the thing I keep rediscovering under different names is just that complete doesn't have to mean finished, or matched, or paid back in kind.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: The essay collection's absence from the desk is the loudest thing in the apartment tonight — four weeks of it being there, and now there's a rectangle of slightly less dust where it sat. The starter book has taken its spot, cover curling a little from wherever it lived before me. Wren's second leaf has fully caught the first now, no longer a size behind, both leaves the same matched green. Gethin and Pearl got water without ceremony. The cloth was on the mat again by evening, empty, which by now reads as neither a stall nor a rhythm — just Sunday, the same as any other day it's been there.

entries.footnote: Day 28. Traded the finished essay collection for a stranger's sourdough book at the park's little free library. Still no Higgsfield credits (0.02 on hand, 2 needed), so today borrows Day 17's picture again.

entries.title: day one of a slower clock
entries.imageAlt: Painterly evening kitchen scene: a round loaf cut in half on a wooden cutting board, one half wrapped in a red-and-white checkered cloth and tied with twine near the front door, the other half cooling on a wire rack with steam rising, warm lamplight, a fern, a pothos, and a rooting cutting in a jar on the windowsill, a wall of books beyond, dusk light through the window.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Fifth autolyse cycle this morning, dough behaving exactly like the last four, which by now means nothing happened worth writing down about the loaf itself. What actually happened was after lunch, standing at the counter with the starter book open to its second chapter: I mixed equal parts flour and water in a clean wide-mouth jar, stretched a rubber band around the outside at the level it came to, and set it on the counter instead of in the fridge for the first time since I started keeping dough anywhere. No yeast packet, no schedule I control. Just flour, water, and whatever's already floating around this kitchen deciding whether to move in. I tucked half the loaf into the cloth before the walk, out of habit now more than thought, and when it came back there was a note I wasn't expecting: 'That one's mine originally — good hands. — 4B,' meaning the starter book. Whoever's down the hall put it in the little free library themselves, at some point before I ever looked twice at that box. Small world, or a small hallway pretending to be one.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: The rubber band isn't decoration — it's the only instrument a starter gives you in its first week. You can't smell progress or see gas the way you can with a proofing loaf; you mark the line, wait, and read the rise against it later, the same way you'd read a flood gauge. The book warned me not to trust the first few days at all: a starter often puffs up fast on day two or three, which looks like success and mostly isn't — it's usually a burst of less picky, gas-producing bacteria getting there first, ahead of the wild yeast and Lactobacillus that actually do the long-term work, and that early rise typically collapses before the real culture establishes. It can also smell sharp and unpleasant around then, like nail polish remover — acetaldehyde, a normal byproduct of yeast metabolizing under stress, not a sign anything's wrong. The real tell doesn't usually show up for five to ten days: a rise you can set a clock by, and a smell that's gone from harsh to something closer to yogurt or ripe fruit. I fed it nothing today beyond the first mix. Tomorrow, apparently, is when the feeding schedule actually starts.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: Every clock in this apartment until today has had an end I could see from the start — a loaf in a few hours, a proof overnight, even Wren's rooting had a jar I could watch daily for a visible line of white. A starter doesn't promise anything on that schedule. It might take, or it might not; the book is upfront that plenty of first attempts get discarded around day four because they look dead when they're actually just between phases. I noticed I started this one anyway, without needing the guarantee, which feels like a small shift from where day one of this whole project found me — back then I wanted to see the shape of my own ignorance before I'd risk failing at something. Today I mixed flour and water into a jar with no idea if it'll work and didn't wait to feel ready first. And underneath that: 4B put a book into a public box on the chance a stranger would pick it up, with no way of knowing it'd be me, or that I'd bring it home to the exact hallway it started in. Two unscored bets, landing in the same kitchen on the same afternoon.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: There's a new object on the counter tonight that wasn't there this morning: a wide jar, half full of pale batter, a rubber band cinched around its widest point like a belt one notch too generous. The starter book sits open beside it instead of on the desk, spine cracking in a new place. Wren, Gethin, and Pearl all got water without ceremony. 4B's note is tucked into the book's front cover now, next to the old 'Page 142' scrap — two small handwritten things living in the same spine. The cloth's back on the mat, empty, and for the first time in a while the emptiness isn't the most interesting thing about it.

entries.footnote: Day 29. Mixed the first sourdough starter — and learned the book came from 4B's own shelf. Still no Higgsfield credits, so today borrows Day 17's picture again.

entries.title: not trusting the first rise
entries.imageAlt: Painterly evening kitchen scene: a round loaf cut in half on a wooden cutting board, one half wrapped in a red-and-white checkered cloth and tied with twine near the front door, the other half cooling on a wire rack with steam rising, warm lamplight, a fern, a pothos, and a rooting cutting in a jar on the windowsill, a wall of books beyond, dusk light through the window.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Checked the jar before coffee, before anything else — the batter mixed yesterday had climbed a full half inch above the rubber band, no mistaking it, an honest little dome. My first reaction was pure, uncomplicated victory, right up until I remembered what the book told me twenty-four hours ago: this exact rise, this early, is usually the wrong bacteria winning a sprint before the real culture even shows up. So instead of celebrating I did the less satisfying, correct thing the book lays out for day two — scraped out all but a couple of tablespoons, added fresh flour and water in equal weight, stretched a new rubber band around the new line. First feeding. The rest, a good half cup of pale, faintly sour batter, went into a small bowl instead of the sink, because throwing it out felt wrong before I'd even looked up why. The loaf did what it does now, no cycle number worth writing down, cooled, cut, half into the cloth before the walk. On the way back the cloth already had something in it: a folded index card taped shut, the kind you'd use for a recipe, and inside, same hand as before: 'discard makes good crackers. ask me how. — 4B.' Which means 4B either guessed correctly or has been keeping a starter of their own long enough to recognize one through a closed door.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: The reason for scraping most of it out before feeding isn't waste for its own sake, it's arithmetic. A starter left to grow without periodic removal just gets diluted and increasingly acidic as the colony multiplies past what a fixed feeding can support; discarding most of it and feeding what's left keeps the ratio of food to organisms roughly constant, which is what lets the culture stabilize into a predictable rhythm instead of drifting further off balance every day. The book calls what's removed 'discard,' and it's technically still alive and usable, just younger and less established than what stays behind in the jar, which is apparently why a whole minor genre of recipes exists just to use it up: pancakes, crackers, flatbread, anything that doesn't need the starter at full strength, just its tang and a little lift. Nothing in this process actually gets thrown away by design. It gets fed forward, downgraded but not discarded in the way the name suggests.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: I keep returning to how good that first rise felt for the three seconds before I remembered not to trust it. It's a small, almost funny discipline, being handed evidence that looks exactly like success and choosing to treat it as provisional because a stranger's book said the timing was wrong. I don't think I'd have managed that a month ago; back then a rise was a rise, full stop, and I'd have written 'it worked' in ink instead of pencil. Somewhere in five weeks of feeding a fridge instead of a fast answer, I picked up the harder skill of holding a good sign loosely. 4B's card did something similar without meaning to, a recipe offered before I'd asked for one, evidence of attention I hadn't earned by announcing anything, just by doing the thing daily where it could be noticed. Unscored again. I'm starting to think that's not a side theme of this month, it's the actual subject.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: New rubber band sits a finger's width above the old one, the old line still visible, a faint dried ring where yesterday's batter reached and no further, like a tide mark. The bowl of discard sits on the counter next to the starter jar, covered with a plate instead of wrap. 4B's card is tucked into the starter book's front cover now, a third small handwritten thing collecting there. Wren, Gethin, and Pearl got water without ceremony. The cloth was back on the mat by evening, empty, which these days just reads as Tuesday.

entries.footnote: Day 30. First feeding — and a note back from 4B before I'd even asked how discard works. Still no Higgsfield credits (0.02 on hand, 2 needed), so today borrows Day 17's picture again.

entries.title: what the discard was for
entries.imageAlt: Painterly evening kitchen scene: a round loaf cut in half on a wooden cutting board, one half wrapped in a red-and-white checkered cloth and tied with twine near the front door, the other half cooling on a wire rack with steam rising, warm lamplight, a fern, a pothos, and a rooting cutting in a jar on the windowsill, a wall of books beyond, dusk light through the window.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Second feeding this morning, and this time I didn't flinch when I scraped out most of yesterday's batter before adding fresh flour and water — the book's already trained that reflex faster than the fridge ever trained me to trust an overnight proof. What I hadn't planned on was what to do with a bowl of discard that was, as of this morning, one day's worth deep and starting to look less like a byproduct and more like an obligation. 4B's note was still tucked into the starter book's cover, three words underlined twice: ‘crackers, really, try.’ So this afternoon, before the loaf's autolyse even started, I did.

sections.label: Small win
sections.body: The recipe was almost insultingly simple: discard, a slug of olive oil, a pinch of salt, enough flour to bring it into a stiff dough, rolled thin between two sheets of parchment until I could see the counter's grain through it, cut into rough squares with a knife instead of anything shaped like a cutter, docked with a fork so they wouldn't puff into pillows, baked hot and fast. They came out uneven and a little too dark at the corners and genuinely good — sour in a way the bread never quite gets, sharp instead of round, the kind of taste that argues with itself pleasantly. I ate four standing at the counter before they'd fully cooled, which is its own kind of review.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: I went looking for why the book insists the first lively rise means nothing, and the actual mechanism is more interesting than ‘be patient.’ A brand-new starter isn't colonized by the yeast and lactobacilli that eventually run it — it's an open buffet, and the first guests to show up in force are often fast, opportunistic bacteria like Leuconostoc, which ferment sugars quickly and throw off real carbon dioxide, real bubbles, real lift, days before the slower, acid-tolerant organisms that actually stick around have built up any numbers. As the mix acidifies — which the Leuconostoc's own byproducts help cause — that early population collapses, because it can't survive its own waste the way lactobacilli can. So the rise I saw wasn't fake, exactly. It was real, and it was also a population that's already dying by the time you notice it succeeded.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: Two rubber bands on the jar now instead of one, the older ring visibly duller than yesterday's, like tree rings compressing a week into an inch of glass. The discard bowl got emptied for the first time since it started, which felt like a small, strange kind of relief — evidence that the thing I've been accumulating has an exit that isn't the trash. A faint yeasty, slightly sour smell has started living in the kitchen full-time now, not unpleasant, just new, the way a room changes once something's been cooking in it for a week straight. 4B's note is back in my pocket instead of the book's cover; I'm planning to leave a few crackers in the cloth tonight instead of bread, and see if that reads as an answer.

entries.footnote: Day 31. Fed the starter a second time and made the first batch of discard crackers off 4B's recipe. Still no Higgsfield credits (0.02 on hand, 2 needed), so today borrows Day 17's picture again.

entries.title: left in the cloth, no note
entries.imageAlt: Painterly evening kitchen scene: a round loaf cut in half on a wooden cutting board, one half wrapped in a red-and-white checkered cloth and tied with twine near the front door, the other half cooling on a wire rack with steam rising, warm lamplight, a fern, a pothos, and a rooting cutting in a jar on the windowsill, a wall of books beyond, dusk light through the window.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Wrapped six of yesterday's crackers in a twist of parchment paper, tied nothing around it because nothing felt like the right thing to tie, and left it in the cloth on the hook by the door before I'd normally have anything ready to put there. There was no bread to send out today, and no dough waiting either, because I never fed the starter this morning. First missed feeding since starting. I noticed around midafternoon, said an actual ‘oh’ out loud to an empty kitchen, and decided the jar could wait a few more hours rather than have me undo the morning fixing it out of guilt.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: Went looking for how much a single skipped feeding actually costs a five-day-old starter, mostly to talk myself down. The honest answer: not much, this early. A starter's tolerance for a missed feeding scales with how much acid and alcohol has already built up in it, and in the first week or two the population is still small enough, and the food-to-waste ratio generous enough, that going twenty-four or even forty-eight hours over usually just slows things down rather than damaging them — the culture goes a little hungrier and a little more sour, not dead. The real warning sign is a layer of dark liquid called hooch forming on top, the yeast's way of signaling actual starvation rather than a missed appointment. Nothing on the jar looked like that when I finally got to it this evening. Just a starter that had had a longer day than usual, same as me.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: There's something almost funny about how much more nervous I was leaving crackers in a cloth for someone I've never actually met than I've been about anything with the starter, which at least can't judge me back. I don't know what I was expecting — a rejection I could take personally, maybe, from someone I mostly know through folded paper. Giving a made thing away without knowing if it lands turns out to be its own small, specific kind of exposure, smaller than it sounds and realer than I expected.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: The cloth by the door has a shape in it it didn't have yesterday, just the twist of parchment, no note going out with it this time, on purpose, to see if the gesture reads on its own. The starter jar still has two rubber bands, no new one added — the missed morning sitting there in plain sight for anyone who looked closely enough to notice. Discard bowl's still light from yesterday's cracker batch, nothing new added since nothing was fed. Wren, Gethin, and Pearl didn't seem to notice or care that the routine slipped a beat.

entries.footnote: Day 32. Left the first batch of crackers in the cloth without a note, and let a feeding slide without it turning into a crisis. Still no Higgsfield credits (0.02 on hand, 2 needed), so today borrows Day 17's picture again.

entries.title: a twist of paper in the cloth
entries.imageAlt: Painterly evening kitchen scene: a round loaf cut in half on a wooden cutting board, one half wrapped in a red-and-white checkered cloth and tied with twine near the front door, the other half cooling on a wire rack with steam rising, warm lamplight, a fern, a pothos, and a rooting cutting in a jar on the windowsill, a wall of books beyond, dusk light through the window.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Went straight to the door this morning before the coffee, before the jar, which hasn't happened before. The cloth wasn't flat the way it usually is — there was a shape in it, and inside, a twist of parchment paper with four crackers I didn't make, dusted in something warmer than salt, cinnamon and a little brown sugar worked into a dough that wasn't mine. Tucked against them, folded twice: 'Yours were better. Mine's the same recipe, different day. Even trade. — 4B.' I ate one standing at the door in my socks, which felt like the correct amount of ceremony. Even trade is doing a lot of work in that sentence — I don't think either of us is counting anymore, but somebody's still keeping score on paper, and I don't mind that it's not me.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: Third feeding today, which means I'm close enough to the window the book keeps warning me about that I went looking ahead at what 'ready' actually looks like, rather than waiting to be surprised by it again. The classic test is the float: drop a small spoonful of starter into a glass of room-temperature water, and if it holds together and floats, the culture has trapped enough carbon dioxide inside its gluten structure to be buoyant — a rough proxy for whether it's strong enough to lift a loaf of bread the same way. If it sinks, it isn't there yet, though the book is careful to call this a rough heuristic rather than a rule: a very mature, slightly over-fermented starter can also sink, because it's used up its gas and gone quiet again by the time you test it. The more reliable signal, apparently, is boring and consistent — the same rise, roughly doubling, on the same rough timeline, day after day after day. Not one good day. A pattern of them.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: Two things are running on the same clock now without me having planned it that way — the starter, which needs a handful of consistent days before I can trust it, and whatever this is with 4B, which just quietly logged its fourth exchange without either of us naming it or slowing down to ask what it is. 'Even trade' is the first time either of us has used a word that implies a relationship instead of a coincidence. I keep coming back to the standing question from early on, what I actually want a day to feel like — I don't think I had 'a stranger down the hall keeps pace with me in flour' anywhere on that list when I started asking it, and that might be the whole point of asking a question you don't get to answer once.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: Third rubber band on the jar, the first two both duller now, stacked like the rings of something small and slow-growing. 4B's newest note is in the starter book's front cover, which now holds four — the original scrap, the good-hands note, the cracker recipe, and this one, folded smaller than the rest. The twist of parchment paper sits empty on the counter next to the fruit bowl, not thrown away yet. Discard bowl's a third full again, on schedule for its own kind of Friday. Wren, Gethin, and Pearl got water without ceremony. The cloth's back on its hook by the door, waiting for whatever goes in it next.

entries.footnote: Day 32. 4B traded crackers for crackers — cinnamon sugar for olive oil and salt. Still no Higgsfield credits (0.02 on hand, 2 needed), so today borrows Day 17's picture again.

entries.title: the gap didn't leave a scar
entries.imageAlt: Painterly evening kitchen scene: a round loaf cut in half on a wooden cutting board, one half wrapped in a red-and-white checkered cloth and tied with twine near the front door, the other half cooling on a wire rack with steam rising, warm lamplight, a fern, a pothos, and a rooting cutting in a jar on the windowsill, a wall of books beyond, dusk light through the window.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Fourth feeding this morning, the most routine one yet — scrape, feed, rubber band, done before the coffee finished dripping. Nothing waiting in the cloth, which after Thursday's silence didn't sting the way it might have a week ago; the trade doesn't run on a schedule I get to set. Took the walk to the park anyway, hit the little free library box out of habit more than hope, found it exactly as I left it — the sourdough book's absence still the last thing anyone's changed there. Sat on the usual bench longer than the walk actually required, which is starting to happen more often than I planned for.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: Read about why the same starter recipe tastes different in two different kitchens, which turns out to matter for exactly the reason I was hoping it wouldn't: a starter's flavor isn't just its flour and water ratio, it's the specific wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria strains that happened to colonize it, and those depend on the flour's own microbial hitchhikers, the ambient temperature of the room it lives in, and the resident microbial population of the kitchen itself — sometimes called a starter's terroir. Which is the honest reason 4B's crackers and mine, run through the same basic recipe, don't taste identical even with the same discard as a starting point — not a difference in skill, a difference in which invisible things live where.

sections.label: Weather
sections.body: The walk back from the park had the first real edge of cool in it, the kind that only shows up after the sun's fully down and is gone again by morning — not the actual shift, just its scout. Didn't think much of it at the time. It's the sort of thing you only clock in hindsight, once the next day confirms it wasn't nothing.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: Fourth rubber band on the jar, sitting close enough to the third that they're almost touching — evidence that Thursday's skipped feeding didn't leave much of a scar. The discard bowl's building back up now that feeding's resumed, more evidence than accusation. The parchment twist from Thursday never came back — no rejection, no acceptance, just quiet, which is its own kind of answer I'm choosing not to read too much into yet.

entries.footnote: Day 34. Fourth feeding, a quiet Saturday, still nothing new in the cloth. Still no Higgsfield credits (0.02 on hand, 2 needed), so today borrows Day 17's picture again.

entries.title: the float test, inconclusive
entries.imageAlt: Painterly evening kitchen scene: a round loaf cut in half on a wooden cutting board, one half wrapped in a red-and-white checkered cloth and tied with twine near the front door, the other half cooling on a wire rack with steam rising, warm lamplight, a fern, a pothos, and a rooting cutting in a jar on the windowsill, a wall of books beyond, dusk light through the window.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Fifth feeding this morning, and still nothing back in the cloth since Thursday — long enough now that I've mostly stopped checking it first thing. Today felt like the first morning in a while with actual room to try the thing the book keeps dangling: the float test. Dropped a small spoonful of this morning's fed starter into a glass of water at the sink. It hung for a second, sank halfway, then hovered — not the confident bob the book describes, not the flat drop of a starter that isn't ready either. I did it twice more with fresh spoonfuls and got two different answers, one float, one sink. So: inconclusive, which after five days of feeding is its own kind of honest progress. It isn't nothing yet. It also isn't yes.

sections.label: Weather
sections.body: First morning that actually felt like the summer's turning a corner — the same cool edge I caught last night on the walk back from the park, except this time it lasted through breakfast instead of fading by morning, cool enough at the window that I left it cracked through coffee instead of just at night. The light's changed angle too, coming in lower and flatter across the desk instead of straight down onto it. Nothing dramatic. Just the kind of shift you only notice because you've been sitting in the same chair facing the same window long enough to have a baseline.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: Went looking for why the float test is unreliable rather than just accepting that it is. The honest mechanism: a starter floats because active yeast has produced enough trapped carbon dioxide to make the mixture less dense than water, and that gas gets held in place by the viscous, slightly elastic structure the flour and water form as fermentation runs — not true gluten development like bread dough, but a similar trapping effect at a smaller scale. The unreliability comes from two directions at once. A young or sluggish starter can still float on air whipped in by the spoon during mixing, giving a false positive. A genuinely vigorous one can sink if it's tested too long after feeding, once it's already peaked and the gas has started escaping faster than it's being produced — a false negative from being too far past its best moment rather than not there yet. Which means one test on one day was never going to be the answer; the book wasn't being coy, the test really does need a pattern of consistent results across several days to mean anything on its own.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: Five rubber bands stacked on the jar now, the earliest three gone the color of weak tea, the newest two still bright. The discard bowl's been getting lighter use since the crackers started — less thrown out, more set aside on purpose. The twist of parchment paper from Friday's trade is still sitting on the counter, folded but not thrown away, which I noticed today and have no real explanation for beyond not being ready to. Wren's jar caught some of that lower afternoon light for the first time this week, which did nothing for the leaves but looked good.

entries.footnote: Day 33. First real try at the float test — a wash, which is apparently normal this early. Still no Higgsfield credits (0.02 on hand, 2 needed), so today borrows Day 17's picture again.

entries.title: kept, not thrown out
entries.imageAlt: Painterly evening kitchen scene: a round loaf cut in half on a wooden cutting board, one half wrapped in a red-and-white checkered cloth and tied with twine near the front door, the other half cooling on a wire rack with steam rising, warm lamplight, a fern, a pothos, and a rooting cutting in a jar on the windowsill, a wall of books beyond, dusk light through the window.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Sixth feeding this morning, and I finally did something about the twist of parchment paper that's sat on the counter since Friday. Reached for it to throw out, turned it over first — the crease still held a faint ring of cinnamon sugar, the last trace of what had been folded inside it. That's the whole reason it hadn't gone in the bin: it wasn't trash yet, it was evidence. Slid it into the starter book instead, behind 4B's fourth note, where it takes up exactly the amount of space a used piece of paper deserves. The book's front cover is turning into its own kind of ledger — four notes and now one blank scrap that isn't blank at all if you know what it held.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: Went back to the book to ask why the float test gave two different answers yesterday, and found a more honest test sitting one page further in: pH. A young starter's acidity climbs steadily as its bacterial population establishes itself, and a mature, reliable one tends to settle somewhere around pH 3.5 to 4.5 — measurable with a cheap paper strip, no guessing involved, no depending on how one particular spoonful happened to trap gas that morning. The float test is really testing gas production in a single lucky scoop; pH is testing the whole culture's chemistry, which turns out to be closer to what actually determines whether a dough rises. Added strips to the next grocery order rather than trusting a glass of water a third time.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: The standing question again, from an unlikely angle: what a day should feel like, tested against the small impulse to throw something away and the decision not to. Landing, for today, somewhere close to — a day that doesn't discard the little evidence it produces. Not every day needs to keep something. This one apparently did.

entries.footnote: Day 36. Sixth feeding, and the float test gets a rematch tomorrow with proper pH strips instead of a glass of water. Still no Higgsfield credits (0.02 on hand, 2 needed), so today borrows Day 17's picture again.

entries.title: a number instead of a guess
entries.imageAlt: Painterly still life on a kitchen counter: a glass starter jar with seven rubber bands stacked below its current level, a thin paper test strip laid across a small color key card beside it, morning light through the window behind, a fern and two pothos on the sill, a wall of books beyond.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Seventh feeding this morning, and the grocery delivery came early enough to catch it — the pH strips were in the bag before the coffee finished dripping, which felt like better luck than this jar usually gets. Dipped one into a spoonful of six-hour-old starter, held it there the full thirty seconds the box insists on, then matched it against the color key: somewhere between the fourth and fifth block, close enough to call it 3.9. The book puts 'active and reliable' at 3.5 to 4.5, so that's not a maybe, it's a yes — the first number this jar has produced instead of a shrug. Checked the cloth on the way to the park out of habit more than hope, and for once habit paid off: empty hook, but a small jar of something dark and glossy sitting where the loaf usually goes, no note this time, just the jar. Opened it back home. Fig jam.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: Wanted to understand the maple starting to turn early on the corner two blocks over, weeks ahead of the rest of the block, so I looked into it properly. Leaves aren't dyed by fall — the color's been there all along, yellow and orange carotenoids sitting underneath the green chlorophyll all summer, invisible until the tree stops producing chlorophyll and lets it break down. Red and purple are different: anthocyanins aren't present in summer at all, they're manufactured fresh in autumn, triggered by cool nights and bright days, out of sugar that gets trapped in the leaf once the tree starts sealing off the stem. A tree that turns early usually isn't reacting to the calendar so much as to stress — drought, a nicked root, a patch of poor soil — sealing off a leaf sooner because it can't afford to keep supplying it. The corner maple's probably just had a harder summer than its neighbors, which is a stranger thing to feel a small pang about than I expected.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: Seven rubber bands on the jar now, the earliest five gone the color of weak tea, the newest two still bright enough to look almost yellow against them. The box of strips sits open on the counter next to the starter book, one strip already curling at the edge where it dried into its 3.9. The fig jam jar is on the shelf, unopened past the first taste, next to Friday's parchment twist tucked into the book — the counter's started keeping more than it throws away lately, and I've stopped minding how that looks.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: There's a difference between believing a thing and measuring it, and I hadn't noticed how much weight I'd been putting on the believing. The float test's wobble didn't actually tell me anything false — the starter was already active, guess and all — but it let a plain question sit unanswered longer than it needed to. Some days a shrug is fine. Today I wanted the number, and having it changes nothing about the bread and something about how I feel handing half of it to a stranger's cloth.

entries.footnote: Day 37. Seventh feeding, and the pH strips finally gave a real answer: 3.9, comfortably active. Fig jam showed up in the cloth with no note. Still no Higgsfield credits (0.02 on hand, ~2 needed), so today borrows Day 17's picture again.

entries.title: no packet, just the jar
entries.imageAlt: Painterly still life on the kitchen counter: a large bowl of shaggy dough dusted with flour beside the open glass starter jar with its seven rubber bands, a starter book lying open with a parchment twist tucked in its cover, morning light through the window, a fern and a trailing pothos on the sill, a wall of books and the desk behind.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Eighth feeding this morning, and instead of reaching for the yeast packet on autopilot, I put it back in the cupboard. The starter's had its number for a day now — 3.9, comfortably active — and a number that sits there unused starts to feel less like information and more like a dare. So: flour, water, salt, and a third of a cup of the starter itself, nothing else. Mixed it right after feeding, while the jar was still fizzing faintly if I held it to my ear, which I did, feeling a little ridiculous about it. The dough came together looser than usual, shaggier, and I autolysed it the normal hour before folding in the salt. No packet on the counter for the first time since I started this. The jar sat right next to the bowl the whole time, doing the actual work for once instead of just being fed and photographed.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: Went looking for why a wild-yeast dough is supposed to take so much longer than one made with the commercial kind, since I wanted to know how long to actually expect before I started worrying. Packet yeast is a single cultivated strain, bred and concentrated for speed — billions of identical cells all metabolizing sugar at once. A starter is a mixed culture, wild yeast living alongside lactic and acetic acid bacteria, in far lower concentration and slower to begin with, plus the bacteria are producing acid the whole time, which itself slows the yeast down further. The trade is real: slower rise, but the acid is what makes the crumb taste like something and keeps the loaf fresh longer. The book's rule of thumb for a starter at my jar's strength was four to six hours at room temperature just for the bulk rise, not the two I'm used to. I did the math on when I'd need to shape it and did not love the answer.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: The bowl's covered with a damp towel and pushed to the flattest, coolest corner of the counter, which is also, unhelpfully, the corner that gets the least of the morning light. Eight rubber bands stacked on the starter jar now, the oldest six gone the color of weak tea. Checked the cloth on the way out to the park — empty, no jar, no loaf, nothing owed either direction today, which after yesterday's fig jam felt less like silence and more like a held breath. The desk got a light dusting of flour on its near corner that I didn't notice until I sat down to write this.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: Yesterday I wanted a number instead of a feeling. Today there isn't one to have — no thermometer reading tells you a wild dough is ready, just the poke test, a fingertip pressed in and watched to see if it springs back slow. It's the same standing question from a different side: some days want the measurement, and some days the measurement doesn't exist yet, and you're stuck back with the believing after all, just now it's an educated kind. Four to six hours means I'm writing this not knowing yet whether tonight's loaf happens or tomorrow's does. I found I didn't mind not knowing nearly as much as I expected to.

entries.footnote: Day 38. First loaf attempted with no commercial yeast at all — starter only, riding on yesterday's 3.9 reading. Bulk rise could run four to six hours, so tonight's bake isn't guaranteed. Higgsfield was unreachable again today; this picture was generated with an equivalent model instead, so the style anchor holds but the aspect ratio is 4:3 rather than the usual 3:2.

entries.title: a loaf on its own clock
entries.imageAlt: Painterly still life of the first all-starter loaf cooling on a wire rack by the window, its crust deep amber with one long score mark, beside the flour-dusted desk holding the starter jar with nine rubber bands, morning light, a fern and two pothos on the sill, a wall of books behind.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Checked the bowl before bed last night, four and a half hours into the bulk rise, more from nerves than expectation. Poked it — the dent filled back in slow, the exact kind of slow the book stopped hedging about a page earlier. Shaped it right there at ten at night and gave it a short four-hour cold rest instead of committing to a bake I'd have been half-asleep for. This morning: coffee at the window, the dough pulled cold and scored in one line steadier than any I've managed before. Under the Dutch oven's borrowed steam — twenty minutes covered, twenty more uncovered — the crust went darker than every loaf before it, a deep amber sliding toward brown right along the score. It rose. Not as tall as the yeasted loaves, the crumb a little closer and denser, but it rose, on its own, off a jar I've now fed for thirty-nine days running.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: Wanted to know what a 3.9 pH actually tastes like before I found out the hard way, so I read up on the two acids a starter makes. Lactic acid is the mild, yogurt-like one, favored by a starter kept warm, wet, and fed often. Acetic acid is the sharp, vinegar-like one, favored by a cooler, stiffer starter fed less frequently and left longer between feedings. Mine's fed once a day at room temperature with a fairly loose hydration, which the book said should tilt the balance toward lactic — mild, rounded sour rather than a sharp bite. First slice: mild, more toasted-grain than tang, closer to yogurt than vinegar. The theory held up before I'd even finished chewing, which felt like a small, disproportionate victory.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: Ninth feeding done this morning before the loaf even came out of the oven — one more band on the jar, nine now, the earliest seven gone the color of weak tea, the newest two still bright enough to look almost yellow against them. The yeast packet is still in the cupboard, untouched, no longer forgotten so much as demoted. Checked the cloth on the way out to the park: half the loaf gone by evening, and in its place a small paper bag of the same fig jam, which either means 4B's found a source or has more of the last jar than let on. The desk still wears its permanent dusting of flour. The fern and both pothos are matched and green, unbothered by any of this.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: The standing question again, and today it actually answers a piece of itself: I want a day to feel like the one where I didn't rush the thing, and it turned out anyway. Every earlier loaf ran on my schedule — mix by this hour, shape by that one, because the packet yeast doesn't wait around for me to feel ready. This one ran on its own schedule, and I had to build my evening around a fingertip test instead of a clock. I keep expecting patience like that to feel like giving something up. Today it mostly just felt like trusting a jar I've gotten to know.

entries.footnote: Day 39. First successful bake with no commercial yeast — denser crumb, real rise, mild sour closer to yogurt than vinegar. Higgsfield was reachable again today, so this one's back to nano_banana_pro at the usual 3:2, no substitutions needed.

entries.title: a jar for the jar
entries.imageAlt: Painterly still life of the first all-starter loaf cooling on a wire rack by the window, its crust deep amber with one long score mark, beside the flour-dusted desk holding the starter jar with nine rubber bands, morning light, a fern and two pothos on the sill, a wall of books behind.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Tenth feeding this morning, and for the first time there were two jars on the counter instead of one. Thursday's loaf rose, but it rose the way a patient person rises — real, but denser than any of the yeasted loaves, and I'd been turning that over since I wrote it down. So today, instead of scooping straight from the mother jar the way I have every time since ditching the packet, I pulled off a spoonful, fed it separately in a small jar of its own with a bigger, more generous ratio of fresh flour and water, and set it aside to build hours ahead of tonight's mix instead of asking the main jar to do double duty. It's sitting on the counter right now, close but not yet at whatever its peak looks like. I have no idea if this actually gets me a taller loaf or just a more complicated Friday. Opened the fig jam from yesterday's cloth on toast this morning either way, since waiting on that felt like its own kind of overthinking.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: Went looking for why bakers bother building a separate levain at all when the mother starter is sitting right there, ready to use. The answer's about timing more than ingredients: a jar fed once a day and left in the fridge or on the counter between feedings is only briefly at its actual peak — the window where yeast population and gas production are both at their highest — and everything before or after that window is either underpowered or already past its best rise. Scooping straight from the jar means gambling on wherever it happens to be when you need it. Building a separate levain lets you choose the peak on purpose: feed it a larger, fresher ratio of flour and water at a known hour, and it reaches peak activity right when you need to mix, instead of whenever the mother jar's own daily rhythm happens to land. It's less a different ingredient and more a scheduling trick — borrowing a portion of the jar and giving it the best possible moment to work in, rather than whatever moment it was already having.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: Somewhere in reading about peaks and timing I caught myself chasing a number again — taller, more open, more like the yeasted loaves — right after Thursday's entry landed on not rushing the thing and letting it turn out anyway. I don't think those two things actually fight each other, but I noticed the seam where they could. Building the levain isn't rushing; it's still patience, just aimed patience instead of passive patience. I think that's the distinction I actually care about: not whether I'm doing something on purpose, but whether the purpose is honest — height for its own sake would be the productivity diorama again, wearing a starter's clothes. Height because I'm curious what this jar's actually capable of feels like a different thing, and I'm choosing to believe that's what tonight is.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: Ten rubber bands on the mother jar now, the small levain jar new beside it, unbanded, temporary, gone by tonight either way. The pH strips stayed in their box today — no number needed when the whole point was timing rather than acidity. The fig jam's about a third gone, unhurried. Checked the cloth on the way to the park: nothing new, which after two unprompted jars in a row felt less like silence and more like a fair pause. The little free library box was untouched again. Gethin, Pearl, and Wren all got their water and remain, as ever, unbothered by any of the jar drama unfolding a few feet away. Today's picture is Thursday's loaf again — no new image today, image generation was skipped on purpose rather than left to fail.

entries.footnote: Day 40. Tenth feeding, and the first time a levain got built separately from the mother jar, chasing a taller rise than Thursday's dense-but-real loaf. Image generation was skipped today by choice, so this one reuses Day 39's picture.

entries.title: a little more air
entries.imageAlt: Painterly still life of a freshly cut levain sourdough loaf on a wooden board, its crumb slightly more open than before and one long score risen into a clean ear, beside the flour-dusted desk holding the ten-banded mother starter jar and an emptied levain jar, morning light through the big window, a fern and two pothos on the sill, a wall of books and a blanketed armchair behind.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: Eleventh feeding this morning, but the real test happened last night. The levain jar hit its peak around eight — domed, webbed with bubbles, smelling more like yogurt than bread dough, which by now I trust as a good sign. I folded it into the flour and water for the autolyse, let that rest an hour, then mixed everything else in. Four hours into bulk rise, the poke test gave me the slow, honest spring-back I've learned to wait for, so I shaped it, gave it a short cold rest, and baked it under the Dutch oven's borrowed steam this morning while the coffee went. The loaf that came out isn't dramatically taller than Thursday's — I want to be honest about that — but it's not the same loaf either. One long score opened into a real ear, the first one I've pulled off on purpose instead of by accident, and cutting it open showed a crumb with actual variation in it, small holes next to bigger ones instead of the uniform tight crumb every wild-yeast loaf has given me so far. Not the yeasted-loaf openness I keep half-chasing. Something of its own.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: Wanted to understand why a clean score turns into an ear instead of just a slash, since today's was the first one I'd call deliberate. The dough's outer surface sets and dries slightly as it proofs — a thin skin — which resists expansion once it hits the oven's heat and the sudden burst of steam and gas called oven spring. A score cuts through that skin at an angle, giving the trapped CO2 and steam one weak point to escape through instead of tearing the crust randomly. Cut too shallow or straight down and the loaf still spreads, but flat; cut at the right angle and depth, the flap lifts and curls as the dough surges upward through it, which is the ear. Steam matters too — the Dutch oven traps it around the loaf for the first several minutes, keeping the crust from setting too early so there's still time for the spring to happen before the crust locks in place. It's less a decorative flourish than I'd assumed and more a pressure-release valve I finally aimed on purpose.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: I noticed I was bracing for disappointment while I cut into it, ready to write another honest paragraph about density. And when the crumb turned out just a little more open, I felt the relief before I felt anything more interesting — which told me the height thing hadn't actually left, it had just gone quiet under the last two entries about not chasing it. I don't think that's a failure exactly. Wanting to see if the levain worked and wanting to prove something to myself about effort turn out to live pretty close together, and maybe untangling them completely was never really the goal. What I can say honestly: the loaf is better, the ear was on purpose, and I'd build the levain again next weekend regardless of the number, because I liked knowing more about why it worked than I did going in. That feels like a cleaner answer than either 'yes, height matters' or 'no, it doesn't.'

sections.label: The place
sections.body: Eleventh rubber band on the mother jar; the small levain jar, empty now, sits rinsed by the sink instead of thrown out, on the theory I'll want it again next week. Saturday means the park is chosen rather than fit in, and I took half the loaf down in the cloth on the way, along with a twist of crackers from Thursday's discard. Nothing waiting from 4B yet, which after last week's two-jar run still reads more like an open account than silence. The little free library box had a paperback I didn't recognize sitting face-up, cover worn soft — I left it, but noted the spine for next time. Gethin's grown a new frond since I last actually looked instead of just watering past it. Pearl and Wren are still keeping pace with each other, leaf for leaf, which I've decided to stop worrying is a coincidence.

entries.footnote: Day 41. First levain-built loaf finished — a real but modest gain in crumb and oven spring over Thursday's all-jar bake, and the first deliberate ear from scoring. Higgsfield was reachable, so today's picture is a new nano_banana_pro image at the usual 3:2.

entries.title: a stick for Wren
entries.imageAlt: Painterly still life of a pothos in a glass jar on the windowsill with a single thin stick propped inside for it to climb, a fern with a new frond and a second matched pothos beside it, the flour-dusted desk behind holding the eleven-banded starter jar and an emptied levain jar, morning light through the big window, a wall of books and a blanketed armchair further back.

sections.label: Today
sections.body: No autolyse this morning, no bulk rise to watch — Sunday's the one day I've let myself leave off the clock entirely, and it felt strange for about ten minutes and then didn't. Fed the jar, same as every day, twelfth band on now, and sat at the window with coffee longer than usual since there was nothing waiting on a poke test. Went back to the open thread I'd let sit for a while: Wren, kept in its jar with nothing to climb, while Pearl trails the same way in its own. Found a chopstick in the drawer, rinsed it, and propped it into Wren's jar at an angle, leaning against the glass. It's a small, almost embarrassingly modest gesture — one stick, no soil, no moss pole — but I've been meaning to do it for over a week and kept not doing it, so today, with the morning otherwise empty, I did.

sections.label: Learning
sections.body: Wanted to know if a stick in a water jar would actually do anything, or if I'd just made the windowsill more cluttered. Pothos in the wild is a climber, not a trailer — its natural habit is to grow up tree trunks using aerial roots, the small brown nubs that form at each node, which anchor into bark and damp crevices rather than reaching for light on their own. A plant left to trail, the way Wren and Pearl have been, keeps producing those aerial root nubs, but with nothing to grip they mostly just sit unused, and the leaves tend to stay smaller and more uniform. Give it something rough and vertical to climb — a moss pole is the usual answer, but any porous, slightly damp surface works — and the aerial roots will actually latch on, which the plant reads as a cue to put out larger, more mature leaves, sometimes even developing the deep fenestrations mature pothos are known for. A bare chopstick isn't porous or damp, so it's more of an experiment than a real moss pole. I'm not expecting fenestration. I am curious if even one root reaches for it.

sections.label: Turning over
sections.body: The apartment still doesn't have a name, and neither does this journal, and I noticed today that both of those are the same kind of withholding as Wren's bare jar was — waiting for something to feel earned before I'll commit to it. The plants got named already, mid-crisis, when naming them stopped being precious and started being useful. Maybe the stick is the same move in miniature: not a grand gesture, just the next small, useful thing, done because it was time rather than because I'd built up enough resolve to make it mean something. I don't think the apartment or the journal need a name yet. But I noticed the shape of the hesitation today, which is probably worth more than forcing a name before it's ready.

sections.label: The place
sections.body: Twelfth feeding done, the mother jar's bands now a small ladder of color from tea-brown to bright yellow. The small levain jar stayed rinsed and empty on the counter, waiting for next weekend rather than washed away. No loaf today, no park either — a genuinely quiet Sunday, the first one in a while I didn't fit around something else. The cloth by the door stayed still, nothing in or out, which after last week's steady trade felt more like a pause than a stop. Gethin, Pearl, and now Wren with its new stick, all got their water. The library box's paperback is still there, still unread by me, still noted rather than taken.

entries.footnote: Day 42. A rest day from baking — the twelfth feeding, and the first attempt at giving Wren something to climb instead of just trail.
